summary: The note describes the Foucault pendulum, a device named after French physicist Léon Foucault that demonstrates Earth's rotation through the slow rotation of its swing plane. It covers Foucault's original 1851 Panthéon experiment and its measured values, the Earth-rotation explanation and latitude dependence, engineering issues, the pendulum's history including relocations and the 2010 cable break, related precession systems, and notable installations worldwide including one at the South Pole.
one_line: Overview of the Foucault pendulum, Léon Foucault's 1851 demonstration of Earth's rotation, its physics, history and installations worldwide.
key_facts: The Foucault pendulum was introduced in 1851 and was the first experiment to give simple, direct evidence of the Earth's rotation.
Foucault followed up in 1852 with a gyroscope experiment to further demonstrate the Earth's rotation.
The first public exhibition of a Foucault pendulum took place in February 1851 in the Meridian of the Paris Observatory.
Foucault's most famous pendulum used a 28-kilogram (62 lb) brass-coated lead bob with a 67-metre long (220 ft) wire suspended from the dome of the Panthéon, Paris.
At the Panthéon's latitude of 48°52'N, the plane of the pendulum's swing made a full circle in approximately 31.8 hours (31 h 50 min), rotating clockwise about 11.3° per hour.
The proper period of the Panthéon pendulum was approximately 16.5 s, so with each oscillation the pendulum rotated by about 9.05×10^-4 rad.
Foucault reported observing 2.3 mm of deflection on the edge of a pendulum every oscillation, which is achieved if the pendulum swing angle is 2.1°.
Foucault published his explanation in an 1851 paper entitled Physical demonstration of the Earth's rotational movement by means of the pendulum in the Comptes rendus de l'Académie des Sciences.
The original bob was moved in 1855 to the Conservatoire des Arts et Métiers in Paris.
On April 6, 2010, the cable suspending the bob in the Musée des Arts et Métiers snapped, causing irreparable damage to the pendulum bob and the marble flooring of the museum.
At the North or South Pole the plane of oscillation stays fixed relative to distant masses while Earth rotates beneath it, taking one sidereal day to complete a rotation.
The angular speed of the swing plane is proportional to the sine of the latitude, ω = 360° sin φ per day, with north latitudes positive.
Heike Kamerlingh Onnes, a Nobel laureate (1913), performed precise experiments and developed a fuller theory of the Foucault pendulum for his doctoral thesis (1879).
Veering of a pendulum was observed in 1661 by Vincenzo Viviani, a disciple of Galileo, who regarded it as a nuisance rather than linking it to Earth's rotation.

The pendulum at the South Pole, installed in a six-story staircase at the Amundsen-Scott South Pole Station, had a length of 33 m (108 ft) and a 25 kg (55 lb) bob and confirmed about 24 hours as the rotation period.
